t: IP to CIDR — Greedy Block Splitting
o: We must cover an inclusive range of $n$ consecutive 32-bit addresses starting at `ip` using the fewest CIDR blocks, covering nothing outside the range. A CIDR block with prefix length $k$ covers exactly $2^{32-k}$ aligned addresses. The key observation: a block starting at address $a$ can have size at most the largest power of two dividing $a$ (alignment), and at most the remaining count $n$. So at each step we greedily take the largest legal block: its size is limited by both alignment of the current start and how many addresses remain. In Example 1, starting at 255.0.0.7 (odd), alignment allows only 1 address → /32; then 255.0.0.8 is divisible by 8 and 9 remain, so take 8 → /29; then 255.0.0.16 covers 1 more → /32. Since $n \le 1000$, even a per-address simulation works, but the greedy emits at most ~$2\log n$ blocks.
k: A CIDR block of prefix k covers 2^(32-k) addresses and must be aligned to a multiple of that size.
The largest valid block at current address a has size min(lowbit(a), remaining n), where lowbit = a & -a.
Greedy largest-block-first yields the minimum number of blocks because any cover must include a block containing the current start, and no larger block is legal there.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute force — one /32 per address
a.i: Since n ≤ 1000, we can simply emit a /32 block for every single address in the range. This trivially satisfies 'cover exactly' but produces n blocks instead of the fewest, so it fails the minimality requirement on strict judges — included only to illustrate the range-to-integer conversion mechanics.
s: Parse ip into a 32-bit integer by shifting each octet.
For each of the n addresses, convert back to dotted form and append addr/32.
a.t: O(n) time — one output line per address.

a.i: At the current start address a, the biggest CIDR block beginning there has size lowbit(a) = a & -a (alignment constraint); it also cannot exceed the remaining count n. Take size = min(lowbit(a), n), emit a block with prefix 32 - log2(size), add size to a, subtract from n. This greedy is optimal: any valid cover's first block starts at a and has size ≤ min(lowbit(a), n), so taking the maximum never hurts later steps.
s: Parse ip into a 32-bit integer x.
While n > 0: compute low = x & (-x); if low == 0 treat as 2^32 (x=0 case).
size = min(low, n); prefix = 32 - (number of trailing zero bits of size).
Append formatted string of x plus '/' + prefix.
a.t: O(log^2 n)-ish — each iteration at least halves n via the power-of-two step, so O(log n) iterations with O(1) work each (plus constant-size formatting).
a.sp: O(log n) for the output list (at most ~2·log₂(n)+1 blocks).

w: Use Approach 2 in interviews — it is optimal and short; mention Approach 1 only to show parsing mechanics before improving it. Pitfalls: (1) forgetting alignment — a block of size 2^t must start at a multiple of 2^t, hence the lowbit cap; (2) when lowbit exceeds remaining n, use the largest power of two ≤ n (i.e., n & -n) rather than just n; (3) overflow — use 64-bit/unsigned arithmetic since ip + n can reach 2^32; (4) x = 0 has lowbit 0, handle specially. Edge cases: n = 1 (single /32), ip ending in .0 or .255, ranges crossing many alignment boundaries. Follow-ups: extend to IPv6, or count minimal blocks without building strings.
